'''Tyrone Poole''' (born February 3, 1972) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who played 13 seasons as a [[cornerback]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He played [[college football]] for the [[Fort Valley State Wildcats]]. He was selected by the [[Carolina Panthers]] 22nd overall of the [[1995 NFL draft]].

Poole has also played for [[Indianapolis Colts]], [[Denver Broncos]], [[New England Patriots]], [[Oakland Raiders]] and [[Tennessee Titans]]. He earned [[Super Bowl ring]]s with the Patriots in [[Super Bowl XXXVIII]] and [[Super Bowl XXXIX]].

In 2011, Poole released a book, "Ultimate Success in the Game of Life," that chronicles his life, going from poverty, to quitting football his senior year at LaGrange High School, to winning the Super Bowl. <ref>{{Cite book |last=Poole |first=Tyrone |url=https://workthatthing.com/products/ultimate-success-in-life-e-book |title=Ultimate Success in the Game of Life |date=January 1, 2011 |publisher=[[Lifebridge Books]] |isbn=978-0984651511 |edition=1st |location=United States |language=en}}</ref>

January 19, 1972) is an American former professional player and [[college football]] who is the running backs coach for [[Illinois Fighting Illini football|Illinois]]. Previously, he served as the head coach of the [[Wayne State Warriors football|Wayne State (MI)]] and as the running backs coach of the [[Denver Broncos]] of the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He played as a [[running back]] for 10 seasons in the NFL. In high school, Wheatley was named [[Michigan]]'s athlete of the year in both football and track and field. He attended the [[University of Michigan]] and earned first-team [[List of All-Big Ten Conference football teams|All-Big Ten Conference]] honors on Big Ten Champion football and track teams. He ranks among the Wolverines' all-time rushing leaders in numerous categories, and his name appears in several places in the Big Ten football record book. He was named to All-Big Ten teams in football and track and field a total of four times, and he earned portions of seven Big Ten championships (two team awards for football, one team award for indoor track, one award for [[110 meter hurdles]], and three awards for individual football statistical performances). Following his graduation from the University of Michigan, Wheatley was selected by the [[New York Giants]] of the NFL in the first round of the [[1995 NFL draft]]. He was traded to the [[Miami Dolphins]], but cut before the [[1999 NFL season|1999 season]] began. He signed with the [[Oakland Raiders]] and led the team in rushing three times, and twice finishing among the NFL's top ten players in rushing [[touchdown]]s. During his NFL career ([[1995 NFL season|1995]]–[[2004 NFL season|2004]]), he totaled over 6,500 all-purpose yards as a running back and [[kickoff returner]]. After retiring from the NFL, Wheatley returned to his hometown to coach his high school alma mater, Hamilton J. Robichaud High School. He has served as the running backs coach for the [[Ohio Northern Polar Bears football|Ohio Northern Polar Bears]], the [[Eastern Michigan Eagles football|Eastern Michigan Eagles]], the [[Syracuse Orange football|Syracuse Orange]] and the [[Michigan Wolverines football|Michigan Wolverines]] on college; and for the [[Buffalo Bills]], the [[Denver Broncos]], and the [[Jacksonville Jaguars]] of the NFL. He has served as the head coach of [[Morgan State Bears football|Morgan State]] and [[Wayne State Warriors football|Wayne State (MI)]].

'''Tyrone Jones''' (August 3, 1961 – June 10, 2008) was a [[gridiron football]] all-star and [[Grey Cup]] champion  [[linebacker]] in the [[Canadian Football League]].<ref name="globe">{{cite news|url=https://www.theglobeandmail.com/sports/former-cfl-star-jones-46-dies-of-cancer/article959654/|title=Former CFL star Jones, 46, dies of cancer|last=Maki|first=Allan|date=2008-06-11|publisher=Globe and Mail|access-date=2008-06-11}}</ref>

Born in [[St. Mary's, Georgia]], Ty's football career began at Camden County High School, Camden County, Georgia. Jones played his [[college football]] at [[Southern University]]. He started his 9-year CFL career in 1983, eventually playing eight seasons with the [[Winnipeg Blue Bombers]] (1983–1987, 1989–1991), one with the [[Saskatchewan Roughriders]] (1992) and one with the [[B.C. Lions]] (1993). Though not drafted by the [[NFL]], he tried out with the [[Phoenix Cardinals]] in 1988, playing one game for them.

He was a four-time CFL and five-time division All-Star. He still holds the Winnipeg career [[quarterback sack|sack]] record (98) along with [[Grey Cup]] records for most sacks in a game (four) and most career Grey Cup sacks (five). He won the [[CFL's Most Outstanding Defensive Player Award]] in 1985 and was on winning Grey Cup teams in 1984 and 1990 (winning the [[Grey Cup Most Valuable Player]] in 1984).<ref name="globe" /><ref name="milk" />

'''Tyronne Kevin Stowe''' (born May 30, 1965) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[linebacker]] for nine seasons in the [[National Football League]] (NFL).

Stowe was born and raised in [[Passaic,  New Jersey]] and played scholastically at [[Passaic High School]].<ref name="PFR1">{{cite web| url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/S/StowTy20.htm |title=Tyronne Stowe Stats |website=Pro Football Reference |access-date=May 25, 2024}}</ref> He played [[college football]] at [[Rutgers University]],<ref name="Sports Career">{{usurped|1=[https://web.archive.org/web/20070208112028/http://www.databasefootball.com/players/playerpage.htm?ilkid=STOWETYR01 Tyronne Stowe Past Stats, Statistics, History, and Awards]}}, databaseFootball.com. Accessed February 19, 2008.</ref><ref name="NFL">{{cite web| url=https://www.nfl.com/players/tyronne-stowe/ |title=Tyronne Stowe Stats |website=NFL.com |access-date=May 25, 2024}}</ref> where he was honored by ''[[The Football News|Football News]]'' as a third-team [[College Football All-America Team|All-American]] as a senior.<ref name="FN 1986">{{cite news |title=All-America News: Football News |newspaper=St. Louis Post-Dispatch |date=November 23, 1986 |page=14D |url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/5716828/allamerica_team_football_news/ |via=Newspapers.com}}{{open access}}</ref>

Stowe signed with the [[San Diego Chargers]] as an [[Free agent#Undrafted free agent|undrafted free agent]], but was cut at the end of the preseason.<ref name="PHN">{{cite news |title=Locals report to NFL |newspaper=The Herald-News (Passaic, NJ) |date=September 24, 1987 |page=C-4 |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-herald-news-locals-report-to-nfl-wa/148045899// |via=Newspapers.com}}{{open access}}</ref> He then joined the [[Pittsburgh Steelers]] as a [[replacement player]] during the [[1987 NFL season#The NFLPA strike|1987 NFLPA strike]].<ref name="PHN"/>

After the strike, the Steelers added him to their regular-season roster, and he remained with them for four years (1987-1990). He followed that with three seasons for the [[Phoenix Cardinals]] (1991-1993), and finished his career with stints in [[Washington Redskins|Washington]] (1994) and [[Seattle Seahawks|Seattle]] (1995-1996).<ref name="PFA">{{Cite web |url=https://www.profootballarchives.com/players/stow00600.html |title=Tyronne Stowe Stats |website=Pro Football Archives |access-date=May 25, 2024 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211205123737/https://www.profootballarchives.com/players/stow00600.html |archive-date=December 5, 2021}}</ref> He spent the 1996 season on the [[injured reserve list]].

He also played for the [[Rhein Fire (NFL Europe)|Rhein Fire]] of the [[World League of American Football]] (WLAF).
